cards.text: Ezekiel the prophet lives among the exiles by the Kebar River (Ezekiel 1:1), and some elders with idols in their hearts just came and sat down in front of him (Ezekiel 14:1-3). Then the word of the LORD comes to Ezekiel again. God tells him to picture a land that sins against Him by acting unfaithfully, and God stretches out His hand against it.

cards.question: God stretches out His hand against that unfaithful land. What's the first thing He says He'll cut off?

cards.text: So it's famine. Then God drops three names into that hungry land: Noah, who built the ark (Genesis 6:14-22), Daniel, taken from Judah to Babylon (Daniel 1:1-6), and Job, the blameless man from Uz (Job 1:1). Friend, that's not a lineup. That's an ALL-STAR TEAM.

cards.question: Noah, Daniel and Job are all in that famine-struck land. Whose lives can their righteousness deliver?

cards.text: Second picture. God sends wild beasts through the land to leave it childless and desolate, and nobody even passes through it for fear of the beasts. That's a road where even the GPS says, "Yeah, we're gonna take a different route."

cards.question: With wild beasts roaming the land, Noah, Daniel and Job could at least deliver their own sons and daughters.

cards.text: Third picture, and it's a sword. God brings it against that land and tells it to pass right through.

cards.question: When God's sword passes through that land, it cuts off the people but leaves the animals alone.

cards.text: Same answer for the sword: the three men alone would be delivered. Fourth picture, and I'm running out of mustache to count on: a plague, with God pouring out His wrath on that land through bloodshed.

cards.question: Even if Noah, Daniel and Job were in that plague-struck land, God says their righteousness could deliver only ___.

cards.text: Four what-ifs, and that answer doesn't budge one crumb. Now God stops talking about "a land" and names a real city, and He says it will be how much worse.

cards.question: God stops speaking about a land in general. Which real city does He name?
Against Jerusalem, God says He will send His ___ dire judgments to cut off both man and beast.

cards.text: Sword, famine, wild beasts and plague. Then God says, "Yet, behold," and friend, the whole room changes.

cards.question: After those four judgments, God says no one at all will be brought out of Jerusalem alive.
God says some survivors will be left in Jerusalem: ___ and ___ who will be brought out.
God says of the survivors from Jerusalem, "They will come out to you." What will bring comfort about the disaster?

answers.text: Hearing the city walls still stand

cards.question: God says those survivors will bring consolation. When people see their conduct, what will they know about all God did in Jerusalem?

answers.text: It was just a stroke of bad luck
It was the enemy acting alone

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 17 quotes "They will come out to you.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: "So it's famine.", "Then God drops three names...", "Friend, that's not a lineup." and "That's an ALL-STAR TEAM." It also carries more than one beat: the famine and the three men.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card says the Daniel of Ezekiel 14:14 is the Daniel taken from Judah to Babylon (Daniel 1:1-6). Ezekiel 14 doesn't say this, and whether the two are the same man is debated. The papa-dorin.md "New people" rule says to say who someone is. The "Leave open what the text leaves open" and "Connecting passages" rules point toward not linking passages the text doesn't link. No rule settles this case.
findings.question: When the passage itself doesn't identify a person, as with the Daniel of Ezekiel 14:14, should Papa Dorin give the traditional identification with a cross-reference, or only name him as the text does?

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: "Second picture.", "God sends wild beasts..." and "That's a road where even the GPS says..."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card says God "tells it to pass right through," as if God speaks to the sword. Ezekiel 14:17 only says God will "say, 'Let a sword pass through it,'" and doesn't say who is being addressed.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card asks whether the sword cuts off both people and animals. "Cut off from it both man and beast" first appears in Ezekiel 14:13 and repeats in 14:17, 14:19 and 14:21, so asking about it at 14:17 asks about a repeated line after its first appearance. No earlier card told the baker about "man and beast" either, so the baker can't reason the answer out.

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: The card asks about "their righteousness could deliver only themselves" at Ezekiel 14:20. The same line first appears in Ezekiel 14:14 and was already asked on card 4. Card 9 also just said "the three men alone would be delivered," which hands the baker the answer.

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: "Four what-ifs" comes right before card 13, which asks the baker to fill in that God will send His "four" dire judgments. The story card gives away the number.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The question quotes "They will come out to you" but never says who "you" is. Nothing on screen tells the baker that the survivors come out to Ezekiel and the exiles.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what.

findings.problem: The question says "When people see their conduct." Ezekiel 14:23 says "when you see their conduct and actions" and is spoken to a specific audience. "People" generalizes the text.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The right answer, "It was not without cause," sounds like Bible wording. "It was just a stroke of bad luck" sounds modern and casual. The right answer stands out by tone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
